title: Man in AI deepfake case admits to stalking women, voyeurism and more
summary: One of two men accused in an AI deepfake case involving 45 alleged victims in Canada and the U.S. — including real-life victims of sexual violence and kidnapping — has pleaded guilty for the role he…

image.caption: Gregry Peter Joseph Van Beek faced seven charges prior to his guilty plea earlier this week, including harassment by watching and besetting, conspiracy to commit an indictable offence and publishing intimate images without consent. (Submitted/Name withheld)

blocks.text: WARNING: This story includes mentions of sexual violence and exploitation, including voyeurism, kidnapping and rape.

One of two men accused in an ongoing multi-jurisdictional investigation into violent and sexual AI deepfake images involving 45 alleged victims in Canada and the U.S. — including real-life victims of sexual violence and kidnapping — has pleaded guilty for the role he played.
Gregry Peter Joseph Van Beek (Vanbeek in court records) is a 39-year-old from West Nipissing, Ont., near Sudbury who often goes by Peter.

He sat in the prisoner's box of an Ottawa courtroom Monday afternoon and admitted to stalking three women in the capital, finding out where they lived and/or worked, taking photographs of two of them through a window, and obtaining photos and videos of others.
Van Beek also published intimate images of two women, made an online threat to rape one of them, and more.
Having these [pictures] is just another way to use her body without consent.Gregry 'Peter' Van Beek

In the commission of his crimes, Van Beek used a now-defunct pornography website called Motherless and the encrypted messaging app Session to communicate with the other man accused in the case, Stephen Lowe. Lowe is a Nova Scotian who is co-operating with police, according to assistant Crown attorney Matthew Brown, who is handling the case with fellow prosecutor Polina Leonov.
Other case moving through court

Lowe is facing 81 charges and remains before the court. He is alleged to have routinely shared biographical data about women with people using Motherless and Session, and invited the users to find and rape them, Brown told the judge in Van Beek's case on Monday.

Two of the stalking victims in Van Beek's case were referred by Lowe, Brown said and records show. Lowe shared with him that two young women were looking for an apartment in Ottawa, "so we know where she'll be as far as city goes, soon."
"F--k that's hot," Van Beek replied. "I'd love to stalk her again."
A message from Van Beek to Lowe, filed in court as evidence. (Ontario Court of Justice exhibit)
Lowe is also alleged to have uploaded 6,889 pieces of media to Motherless, which were viewed more than 1.5 million times, Brown said.

The charges against Lowe include 28 counts of criminal harassment, 26 counts of uttering threats to cause bodily harm, 24 counts of making and publishing obscene materials, and three counts of possessing, making and distributing child sexual abuse and exploitation material.
The allegations against Lowe have not been proven. His next court appearance is scheduled in December.
Images of unidentified girls shared
The facts against Van Beek came from Lowe's devices and website records handed over to police in response to production orders.
On Monday, Van Beek pleaded guilty to criminal harassment by watching and besetting, publishing intimate images of two women without their consent, and uttering a threat to cause bodily harm.

blocks.text: Other agreed facts read out by the Crown included that Van Beek talked about personally recording women without their consent. He admitted going to a mall in Ottawa to "shoot creepshots" between 2009 and 2014, and admitted to finding girls at West Nipissing high schools and finding their friends on social media, Brown told court.

He sent 12 photographs of an unidentified teenage girl taken in a grocery store, as well as photos of her in a bathing suit taken from her social media, Brown said. Van Beek also sent 16 photos of another unidentified teenage girl at a hotel, and wrote that she caught him looking at her a few times and "looked uncomfortable."
'Fun' to focus on 'real life victims'
Van Beek and Lowe also wrote about wanting to rape victims of serial killers, kidnappings, rape and suicide, Brown said. Van Beek wrote that "it's fun" to fantasize about "real life victims."
The woman depicted in one of the intimate images Van Beek published is one such real-life victim of kidnapping and sexual violence.
Details about what happened to her, and her life since, cannot be published because they could identify her and breach a routine court-ordered publication ban that protects victims.

Van Beek found more than 50 "boudoir" photographs of her in lingerie with some nudity. He explained to Lowe that for years, he's browsed online services used by professional photographers to upload and house images to send to their clients, and found instances where photographers hadn't adequately privatized them.

"Anyway I've collected hundreds, women from all walks of life, wives, nurses, teachers etc. ... some have been somewhat famous like news women, wives of major athletes or social media influencers," he explained to Lowe. "Long story short it's not like they are meant to be public but you can find them with some work. I've done that for years and am in some private online groups where I trade finds with others."
"Lucky would be the guy who kidnapped and raped her now!" Lowe wrote.
"Having these is just another way to use her body without consent," Van Beek replied.

Police spoke to Van Beek's wife during the investigation, Brown told court. She told them Van Beek had admitted to her back in 2017 that he was interested in voyeurism, and that she thought it had stopped.
'Underground fantasy behaviours'
Van Beek's defence lawyer James Foord stood in front of the judge after the Crown finished speaking and said the facts against his client were accurate, but he wished to comment.

His client, who has no criminal record and had never been in trouble with the law before, had "no knowledge" of any deepfake pornography images allegedly created by Lowe. "That was Mr. Lowe," Foord said.
In messages between Lowe and Van Beek filed in court, Van Beek told Lowe he had seen Lowe's AI content. It's unclear what content he had seen specifically.

Van Beek was involved in "underground fantasy behaviours," Foord said. And "one of the difficulties" in Van Beek's case is that the things he said online didn't always reflect what he did or what he was going to do, Foord added.
"It wasn't entirely masturbatory fantasy," Ontario Court Justice David Berg countered.
"It almost entirely was," Foord replied.
Van Beek and his wife attended couples therapy together after he admitted to voyeurism. Van Beek also sought individual therapy for his voyeurism addiction and managed to quit, Foord added.
"Unfortunately," Van Beek later returned to voyeurism, Foord said. Van Beek's wife continues to support him nonetheless, and Van Beek is committed to getting help, Foord concluded.
James Foord, seen here in 2019, is a criminal defence lawyer and past president of the Defence Counsel Association of Ottawa. (Laura Osman/CBC)
'There's a lot of context': Van Beek
The judge turned his attention to Van Beek and asked if he agreed to the lengthy facts read out by the Crown. Van Beek hesitated and looked at his lawyer.
As Berg began to ask Van Beek to look at him instead, Van Beek replied, "Yeah. Yes.... There's a lot of context, but yes."
"But the criminal behaviours that are described in here," Berg began to say.
"Yes," Van Beek said. "The four counts, yes."
Regardless of Monday's plea, the investigation into Van Beek continues. Court heard that police are still trying to unlock all the electronic devices seized from Van Beek when he was arrested in May.
If police do gain access to Van Beek's devices, it's possible more charges could be laid.
A sentencing hearing will take place in the new year. In the meantime, a sexual behaviours assessment has been ordered for Van Beek while he remains in jail.
Sexual violence resources
If you're in immediate danger, call 911.
For support in your area, you can find crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada, which maintains a database for every province and territory.
